source.text: דְּבַר־יְהוָ֣ה׀אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָיָ֗ה אֶל־הוֹשֵׁ֨עַ֙ בֶּן־בְּאֵרִ֔י בִּימֵ֨י עֻזִּיָּ֥ה יוֹתָ֛ם אָחָ֥ז יְחִזְקִיָּ֖ה מַלְכֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֑ה וּבִימֵ֛י יָרָבְעָ֥ם בֶּן־יוֹאָ֖שׁ מֶ֥לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] word of Yahweh which came to Hosea son of Beeri in [the] days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in [the] days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel.

en.L: The word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} which came to Hosea son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel.
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}}'s word came to Hosea son of Beeri during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah over Judah, and during the reign of Jeroboam son of Joash over Israel.
en.R: This is the message {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave to Hosea son of Beeri. It came while Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah were kings of Judah, and while Jeroboam son of Joash was king of Israel.

decisions.choice: the kings named date Hosea's work to the eighth century BC, from the last years of Jeroboam II into the reign of Hezekiah
decisions.reason: Jeroboam son of Joash is Jeroboam II, who ruled the northern kingdom of Israel from about 793 to 753 BC (2 Kings 14:23-29), not Jeroboam son of Nebat, Israel's first king. The kings of Judah named are the same four as in Isaiah 1:1: Uzziah (about 792-740 BC), Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (who began to reign about 715 BC). So Hosea spoke from the prosperous last years of Jeroboam II, through the turmoil that followed, and probably past the fall of Samaria to Assyria in 722 BC. The heading names only one king of Israel, although six more reigned after Jeroboam before the kingdom ended (2 Kings 15:8-17:6). It does not say why; the list of Judah's kings carries the dating on.

decisions.choice: Hosea son of Beeri: the prophet, known only from this book
decisions.reason: Nothing is known of Hosea or his father Beeri beyond this book. His name means "salvation" or "he has saved", from the same root as the names Joshua and Jesus. It is spelled the same as the name of Hoshea, the last king of Israel (2 Kings 17:1). Hosea is the only one of the writing prophets who came from the northern kingdom and spoke mainly to it.

decisions.choice: the word of the LORD that came to Hosea: the heading of the whole book
decisions.reason: The same heading opens Joel, Micah and Zephaniah. It presents everything that follows, the account of Hosea's marriage and the poems, as one message from the LORD, given through a particular man at a particular time.

decisions.choice: The word of the LORD which came to (L); The LORD's word came to (B); in the days of (L), during the reigns of (B), while ... were kings (R)
decisions.reason: The heading follows the wording set for the Twelve, which follows the Jeremiah table for dated headings: "in the days of X" at Literal, "during the reign of X" at Balanced, "while X was king" at Readable. Literal lists the kings of Judah without "and", as the Hebrew does. Readable splits the long heading into two sentences.

source.text: תְּחִלַּ֥ת דִּבֶּר־יְהוָ֖ה בְּהוֹשֵׁ֑עַפוַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוָ֜ה אֶל־הוֹשֵׁ֗עַ לֵ֣ךְ קַח־לְךָ֞ אֵ֤שֶׁת זְנוּנִים֙ וְיַלְדֵ֣י זְנוּנִ֔ים כִּֽי־זָנֹ֤ה תִזְנֶה֙ הָאָ֔רֶץ מֵֽאַחֲרֵ֖י יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] beginning of [the] speaking of Yahweh through Hosea: and said Yahweh to Hosea, Go, take for yourself a wife of prostitutions and children of prostitutions, for surely prostitutes itself the land, from after Yahweh.

en.L: The beginning of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s speaking through Hosea: {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to Hosea, "Go, take yourself a wife of prostitution and children of prostitution, for the land utterly prostitutes itself, [turning] from following {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."
en.B: When {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} first spoke through Hosea, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "Go, marry a promiscuous wife and have children born of promiscuity, for the land is wholly given to prostitution; it has turned away from following {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."
en.R: This is how {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} began to speak through Hosea. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "Go and marry a wife who will be unfaithful, and have children born of unfaithfulness. That is what the people of this land have done. They have been completely unfaithful to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and have stopped following {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

decisions.choice: a wife of prostitution: a woman marked by sexual unfaithfulness; the text does not say whether she was already unfaithful when Hosea married her or became so afterward
alternatives: a woman already unfaithful before the marriage
a woman who would become unfaithful after it
a woman of an unfaithful people
decisions.reason: The phrase does not mean that she was a professional prostitute; the word for a prostitute is not used. The plural noun describes a habit or character of unfaithfulness. Some read the command as it stands: Hosea was told to marry a woman already known to be unfaithful, as a living picture of the LORD's bond with an unfaithful people. Others read it as told looking back: Hosea married Gomer, she later proved unfaithful (as chapter 2 and 3:1 suggest), and the command describes her as she turned out to be. A third reading takes the phrase as belonging to the whole people: any wife Hosea took from this land would share its unfaithfulness to God. The text does not settle the question.

decisions.choice: prostitute oneself: be sexually unfaithful; used of a people's worship of other gods
decisions.reason: The verb is used for sexual unfaithfulness and, very often, for Israel's turning to other gods, pictured as a wife leaving her husband (Exodus 34:15-16; Judges 2:17; Jeremiah 3:1). In Hosea the two senses run together: the prophet's marriage is the picture, and the people's worship of the Baals (2:10, 15) is the reality. The verb is doubled here ("prostituting, it prostitutes itself"), which makes it emphatic.

decisions.choice: the land ... from after the LORD: the people of the land have stopped following the LORD
decisions.reason: "The land" stands for the people who live in it. To walk "after" the LORD is to follow him as his people (Deuteronomy 13:5; Jeremiah 2:2). The land has turned away "from after" him to follow others.

decisions.choice: children of prostitution: children born to such a wife, sharing the name of the unfaithful people
decisions.reason: "Take" governs both the wife and the children: the children come with the marriage. They are called this because of their mother, not for anything they have done. The book does not say plainly whether all three were Hosea's own; 1:3 says that Gomer bore the first son "to him", and 1:6 and 1:8 do not repeat the words.

decisions.choice: the beginning of the LORD's speaking through Hosea: the first part of the LORD's word to Hosea
decisions.reason: The phrase introduces the account of the marriage as the starting point of Hosea's work. The small word translated "through" can also mean "with" or "to" (as Numbers 12:6, 8); "through" fits a heading about the LORD speaking by means of the prophet, whose marriage itself becomes the message.

decisions.choice: a wife of prostitution (L); a promiscuous wife (B); a wife who will be unfaithful (R); prostitutes itself (L, B); unfaithful (R)
decisions.reason: The wording settled for Hosea in the terms note. Readable's "will be unfaithful" says what the marriage would bring; it does not decide whether she had been unfaithful before (m1). Readable says "unfaithful" for the verb, as in Judges 2:17, and spells out that the people of the land have done what the marriage pictures.

decisions.choice: marry (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Take a wife" is the ordinary Hebrew way of saying "marry". Literal keeps "take for yourself".

source.text: וַיֵּ֨לֶךְ֙ וַיִּקַּ֔ח אֶת־גֹּ֖מֶר בַּת־דִּבְלָ֑יִם וַתַּ֥הַר וַתֵּֽלֶד־ל֖וֹ בֵּֽן׃

records.literal_gloss: And he went and took Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore to him a son.

en.L: So he went and took Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore to him a son.
en.B: So Hosea went and married Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she became pregnant and bore him a son.
en.R: So Hosea married Gomer daughter of Diblaim. She became pregnant and gave birth to Hosea's son.

decisions.choice: Gomer daughter of Diblaim: a real woman, named with her father
decisions.reason: Gomer and Diblaim are named nowhere else. The account gives her name and her father's name as it would for anyone, so the marriage is told as something that happened, not as a story invented only to make a point. Unlike the children's names, her name is not explained.

decisions.choice: bore him a son: the first child is said to be Hosea's
decisions.reason: The words "to him" are not repeated for the daughter (1:6) or the second son (1:8). Some take this to hint that the later children were not Hosea's, which would fit "children of prostitution" (1:2; 2:6). The text does not say so directly.

decisions.choice: Hosea (B, R); married (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Hosea where the Hebrew says "he", and say "married" for "took" (as 1:2).

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ אֵלָ֔יו קְרָ֥א שְׁמ֖וֹ יִזְרְעֶ֑אל כִּי־ע֣וֹד מְעַ֗ט וּפָ֨קַדְתִּ֜י אֶת־דְּמֵ֤י יִזְרְעֶאל֙ עַל־בֵּ֣ית יֵה֔וּא וְהִ֨שְׁבַּתִּ֔י מַמְלְכ֖וּת בֵּ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Yahweh to him, Call his name Jezreel, for yet a little and I will visit the bloods of Jezreel on [the] house of Jehu, and I will put an end to [the] kingdom of [the] house of Israel.

en.L: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "Call his name Jezreel, for in yet a little [while] I will visit the blood of Jezreel on the house of Jehu, and I will make the kingdom of the house of Israel cease.
en.B: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "Name him Jezreel, for in a little while I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood shed at Jezreel, and I will bring the kingdom of the house of Israel to an end.
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to Hosea, "Name him Jezreel. Soon I will punish the family of King Jehu for the people they killed at Jezreel. I will bring the kingdom of Israel to an end.

decisions.choice: Jezreel: a town and valley where Jehu seized the throne in bloodshed; the name means "God sows"
decisions.reason: Jezreel was a royal town of the northern kingdom, above the great valley of the same name. There Jehu killed King Joram, Queen Jezebel and the family of Ahab, and so took the throne (2 Kings 9:14-10:11). Jeroboam II, king when Hosea began (1:1), was Jehu's great-grandson. The LORD had promised Jehu that his sons would rule to the fourth generation (2 Kings 10:30), and Jeroboam's son Zechariah was killed after six months as king, ending Jehu's line (2 Kings 15:8-12). The name itself means "God sows". Here it recalls bloodshed; in 2:2 and 2:24-25 the meaning "God sows" turns it into a promise.

decisions.choice: visit the blood ... on: punish for the bloodshed
decisions.reason: "Visit" something on someone means to call them to account for it, to bring its consequences on them (Exodus 20:5; Hosea 2:15). "Bloods" is plural, the usual Hebrew way of speaking of blood that has been shed.

decisions.choice: the LORD punishes Jehu's house for the killings at Jezreel, although 2 Kings 10:30 praises Jehu for ending Ahab's house
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 10:30 says that Jehu did what was right in the LORD's eyes in destroying Ahab's family, and 10:31 adds that he did not walk in the LORD's law with all his heart. Hosea does not explain how the two judgments fit. Some readers think the blood is condemned because Jehu went beyond what he was told, killing also the king of Judah and his relatives (2 Kings 9:27; 10:12-14); others think that his dynasty, having kept the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, now bears the guilt of how it began. The text names the bloodshed and leaves the reason unstated.

decisions.choice: the kingdom of the house of Israel: the northern kingdom, which ended when Assyria took Samaria in 722 BC
decisions.reason: "The house of Israel" here is the northern kingdom, distinct from Judah (1:7). Within about thirty years of Jeroboam II's death it was conquered by Assyria and its people were taken away (2 Kings 17:5-6).

decisions.choice: punish ... for the blood shed at Jezreel (B); punish ... for the people they killed at Jezreel (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "visit the blood of Jezreel" means (m2). Readable adds "King" to Jehu and says "family" for "house". "Jezreel" is kept at every level, with the meaning of the name in the footnote (m1).

source.text: וְהָיָ֖ה בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא וְשָֽׁבַרְתִּי֙ אֶת־קֶ֣שֶׁת יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל בְּעֵ֖מֶק יִזְרְעֶֽאל׃

records.literal_gloss: And it will be in the day the that, and I will break [the] bow of Israel in [the] valley of Jezreel.

en.L: And it will be on that day [that] I will shatter the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel."
en.B: On that day I will break Israel's bow in the valley of Jezreel."
en.R: At that time I will break Israel's bow in the valley of Jezreel. I will destroy the power of their army."

decisions.choice: break the bow of Israel: destroy Israel's military power
decisions.reason: The bow, the weapon of the archer, stands for strength in war (1 Samuel 2:4; Jeremiah 49:35). To break it is to leave a nation defenseless. In 2:20 the LORD will break bow and sword and war themselves, so that his people can live in safety.

decisions.choice: the valley of Jezreel: the broad plain of northern Israel, a battlefield in many wars
decisions.reason: The plain below the town of Jezreel was the easiest route through the hills and saw many battles (Judges 6:33; 1 Samuel 29:1; 31:1-7). The place where Jehu's house began in blood will see Israel's army broken. The verse does not name the battle.

decisions.choice: I will destroy the power of their army
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the picture of the bow and adds a sentence saying what it stands for (m1). The quotation that began in verse 4 closes here.

source.text: וַתַּ֤הַר עוֹד֙ וַתֵּ֣לֶד בַּ֔ת וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֔וֹ קְרָ֥א שְׁמָ֖הּ לֹ֣א רֻחָ֑מָה כִּי֩ לֹ֨א אוֹסִ֜יף ע֗וֹד אֲרַחֵם֙ אֶת־בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כִּֽי־נָשֹׂ֥א אֶשָּׂ֖א לָהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And she conceived again and bore a daughter, and he said to him, Call her name Lo-ruhamah, for not I will again any more have compassion on [the] house of Israel, that surely I should forgive them.

en.L: And she conceived again and bore a daughter. And he said to him, "Call her name Lo-ruhamah, for no longer will I again have compassion on the house of Israel, that I should in any way forgive them.
en.B: Gomer became pregnant again and gave birth to a daughter. Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to Hosea, "Name her No Compassion, for I will no longer show compassion to the house of Israel or forgive them in any way.
en.R: Gomer became pregnant again and gave birth to a daughter. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to Hosea, "Name her No Compassion. I will not show compassion to the people of Israel anymore. I will not forgive them at all.

decisions.choice: Lo-ruhamah: "not shown compassion", "not pitied"
decisions.reason: The name is made of "not" and a form of the verb that means to show compassion, the tender love of a parent for a child (Psalm 103:13; Isaiah 49:15). The child's name announces the LORD's word about Israel: the compassion he had shown them is withdrawn. The verb returns in the same verse, "I will no longer have compassion", and in 2:3, 6 and 25, where the name is reversed.

decisions.choice: that I should in any way forgive them
alternatives: but I will surely take them away
decisions.reason: The last words are hard. The verb usually means "lift" or "carry", and "lift for them" can mean "forgive them" (as Genesis 18:24, 26). Read that way, the clause continues the sentence: no compassion, so no forgiveness at all. The same verb can also mean "carry away", and some take the clause as a new threat: "I will surely take them away", into exile. The forgiveness reading follows the usual sense of the verb with "for" a person; the other reading is possible.

decisions.choice: he said to him: the LORD said to Hosea
decisions.reason: The Hebrew does not name the speaker or the hearer, but the pattern of 1:2 and 1:4 makes them plain.

decisions.choice: No Compassion (B, R); Lo-ruhamah (L)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable translate the name, by the founder's ruling for Hosea, because the book turns on what the names mean and 2:3 and 2:25 reverse them. Literal keeps the Hebrew name, with its meaning in the footnote (m1). "Compassion" is kept for the name and for the verb in the same sentence, so the reader can see the name explained. Isaiah keeps Maher-shalal-hash-baz at every level; Hosea differs on purpose.

source.text: וְאֶת־בֵּ֤ית יְהוּדָה֙ אֲרַחֵ֔ם וְהֽוֹשַׁעְתִּ֖ים בַּיהוָ֣ה אֱלֹֽהֵיהֶ֑ם וְלֹ֣א אֽוֹשִׁיעֵ֗ם בְּקֶ֤שֶׁת וּבְחֶ֨רֶב֙ וּבְמִלְחָמָ֔ה בְּסוּסִ֖ים וּבְפָרָשִֽׁים׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] house of Judah I will have compassion on, and I will save them by Yahweh their God, and not I will save them by bow and by sword and by battle, by horses and by horsemen.

en.L: But on the house of Judah I will have compassion, and I will save them by {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} their God; and I will not save them by bow, or by sword, or by battle, by horses or by horsemen."
en.B: But I will show compassion to the house of Judah, and I will save them by {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} their God. I will not save them by bow or sword or battle, or by horses and horsemen."
en.R: But I will show compassion to the people of Judah. I, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} their God, will save them {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}}. I will not save them by war, with bows and swords, horses and horsemen."

decisions.choice: by the LORD their God: the LORD speaks of himself by name
decisions.reason: The LORD is speaking, yet he says "by the LORD their God" rather than "by myself". Using his own name stresses who the rescuer is: Judah's safety will come from the God of the covenant, not from its own strength. Prophets often let God speak of himself in this way (Isaiah 45:3; Zechariah 10:12).

decisions.choice: not by bow, sword or battle: rescue that does not depend on weapons
decisions.reason: The list piles up the means of war, then sets them aside. The same conviction is in Psalm 20:8 and Isaiah 31:1: a people that trusts horses and chariots is not saved by them. The verse does not say when Judah would be rescued. Readers have often thought of Jerusalem's escape from the Assyrian army in Hezekiah's time (2 Kings 19:32-36), but the text does not name it.

decisions.choice: show compassion (B, R)
decisions.reason: The verb is the one in the name No Compassion (1:6). Judah receives what Israel loses. Balanced and Readable say "show compassion", matching the name.

decisions.choice: I, the LORD their God, will save them myself
decisions.reason: Readable turns the LORD's third-person reference to himself into "I, the LORD their God", so that the reader does not think another person is meant (m1). It lists bow, sword, horses and horsemen as the means of war.

source.text: וַתִּגְמֹ֖ל אֶת־לֹ֣א רֻחָ֑מָה וַתַּ֖הַר וַתֵּ֥לֶד בֵּֽן׃

records.literal_gloss: And she weaned Lo-ruhamah, and she conceived and bore a son.

en.L: And she weaned Lo-ruhamah, and she conceived and bore a son.
en.B: After Gomer had weaned No Compassion, she became pregnant and gave birth to a son.
en.R: After Gomer stopped nursing No Compassion, she became pregnant again and gave birth to a son.

decisions.choice: weaned: the time between the children was some years
decisions.reason: Mothers nursed their children much longer than is common today; Hannah kept Samuel at home until he was weaned and then brought him to the house of the LORD (1 Samuel 1:22-24), and weaning was often at two or three years. The note marks the passing of time between the second and third child.

decisions.choice: No Compassion (B, R); Lo-ruhamah (L)
decisions.reason: The name is translated at Balanced and Readable and kept in Hebrew at Literal, as in 1:6. Readable says "stopped nursing" for "weaned" and adds "again", which the verb implies.

source.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר קְרָ֥א שְׁמ֖וֹ לֹ֣א עַמִּ֑י כִּ֤י אַתֶּם֙ לֹ֣א עַמִּ֔י וְאָנֹכִ֖י לֹֽא־אֶהְיֶ֥ה לָכֶֽם׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And he said, Call his name Lo-ammi, for you [are] not my people, and I not will be to you.

en.L: And he said, "Call his name Lo-ammi, because you [are] not {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people, and I will not be yours."
en.B: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, "Name him Not My People, because you are not {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people, and I will not be yours."
en.R: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, "Name him Not My People. You are not {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people, and I will not be your God."

decisions.choice: Lo-ammi: "not my people"
decisions.reason: The name is made of "not" and "my people". The words that follow explain it. Its reversal is promised in 2:1, 3 and 25.

decisions.choice: you are not my people, and I will not be yours: the covenant promise turned around
decisions.reason: The covenant was summed up in the words "I will be your God, and you will be my people" (Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12). Here both halves are denied. The verb "I will be" is the same form God uses when he gives his name to Moses, "I am who I am" (Exodus 3:14), and the words can also be heard as "I am not 'I AM' to you". Either way, the relationship that made Israel the LORD's people is declared broken.

decisions.choice: he said ... you: the LORD speaks to Israel through the child's name
decisions.reason: The speaker is the LORD, as in 1:4 and 1:6. "You" is plural: it addresses the people, not the child.

decisions.choice: Not My People (B, R); Lo-ammi (L)
decisions.reason: As in 1:6, Balanced and Readable translate the name and Literal keeps the Hebrew with the meaning in the footnote (m1).

decisions.choice: I will not be your God
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "I will not be to you". Readable supplies "God" from the covenant words the sentence echoes (m2); Literal and Balanced say "I will not be yours".
